crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is a structured review of how an organisation's finance function actually uses artificial intelligence, covering the tools in play, the data they touch, and the controls around them.

children.name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
children.blurb: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls that stop ledgers, payroll files, deal documents and client records from being pasted into consumer chatbots or uploaded to third party AI services.

children.name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Model risk and bias testing covers the checks an organisation runs on a model before and after it goes into use, to see whether it produces wrong, unstable or unfairly skewed outputs.

children.name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
children.blurb: Mapping financial AI to the rules is the work of connecting each model, tool or automated decision in a finance function to the specific regulation, accounting standard or supervisory expectation that governs it.

children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped deployment covers AI systems that run on hardware the organisation controls, with no dependency on an outside network.

sections.body: Governance, risk and financial data security is the part of AI accounting work that asks whether a system can be trusted with money, records and obligations before anyone relies on its output. In practice this means auditing how AI tools are enabled across a finance function, checking what data leaves the building when staff paste figures into a chatbot, testing models for drift and bias, and matching each use case to the rules that apply to it. The work is concrete: reviewing access logs, tracing where prompts and files travel, running test cases against a model to see how it behaves on edge inputs, and deciding whether a workload belongs on a public endpoint or inside a controlled environment. It sits between finance, IT, risk and compliance, and it is usually the step that decides whether an AI tool gets rolled out or quietly shelved.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this are settled. Data leakage through public models is well understood, and the controls are mostly procedural: block sensitive inputs, use enterprise endpoints, log and review usage. Model risk testing has borrowed methods from credit and market risk, so validation, backtesting and monitoring have a shape that auditors recognise, even if the tests themselves are still being adapted to language and generative systems. What is not solved is the mapping problem. Rules differ by jurisdiction, change often, and rarely name AI directly, so a firm has to interpret principles written for other technologies and defend that reading. Bias testing is the weakest area, because fairness has no single agreed measure and results depend heavily on the data and the definition chosen. Local and air-gapped deployment solves the leakage question but creates new ones around updates, support and cost, and none of these controls remove the need for a human who understands the numbers.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here follow the order in which a finance team usually meets these problems. The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is the starting point, covering how to find out what tools are already in use and what they touch, which is the question most organisations cannot answer at first. Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models then deals with the most immediate exposure, the movement of figures and documents into systems the firm does not control. Model Risk and Bias Testing goes deeper into the model itself, looking at validation, monitoring and the harder question of whether outputs are fair and stable. Mapping Financial AI to the Rules takes the findings from those pages and connects them to regulatory obligations, which is where interpretation and documentation matter most. Local and Air-Gapped Deployment is the control option that answers several of the earlier concerns at once, and a reader goes there when the decision is not whether to use AI but where to run it. Read together, they move from discovery to containment to testing to compliance to architecture.
